summary: Euphrosyne is a goddess of ancient Greek religion and mythology, one of the Charites (Graces), the personification of mirth, joy, and good cheer. According to Hesiod's Theogony she was a daughter of Zeus and the Oceanid Eurynome, and a sister of the other two canonical Graces, Aglaea and Thalia. The Charites were minor goddesses of charm, beauty, and festivity who attended Aphrodite, and Euphrosyne's name itself means "merriment." She is also sometimes called Euthymia ("good mood") or Eutychia ("good luck").
etymology: From the Ancient Greek Euphrosyne (Εὐφροσύνη), formed from euphrosynos, "merry" or "cheerful" (eu, "good," + phren, "mind"). The name thus means "merriment" or "good cheer."

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: According to Hesiod's Theogony, Euphrosyne and her sisters Thalia and Aglaea were the daughters of Zeus and the Oceanid nymph Eurynome. These three formed the canonical set of Charites, or Graces.
Other genealogies were also recorded in antiquity. Euphrosyne is variously named a daughter of Zeus by Eurydome, Eurymedousa, or Euanthe; of Dionysus and Coronis; or of Helios and the Naiad Aegle.

A distinct figure of the same name appears in the Fabulae of the Roman author Hyginus, who lists a Euphrosyne among the offspring of Nox (Night) and Erebus (Darkness). This Euphrosyne is reckoned a separate personification from the Grace, belonging to the brood of abstract powers descended from Night.

sections.heading: Role and personification
paragraphs: Euphrosyne was one of three sisters who together personified grace, charm, and beauty. As a group the Charites embodied festivity and the delights of social life, and they were closely associated with Aphrodite, the goddess of beauty, whom they were said to attend.

Euphrosyne in particular personified good cheer, joy, and mirth. The poet Pindar described the Graces as created to fill the world with pleasant moments and goodwill, and their domains extended to dance, song, banquets, and the gracious pleasures that adorn human gatherings.

sections.heading: Worship
paragraphs: Euphrosyne was venerated together with her sisters rather than as an independent cult figure. The principal worship of the Charites is associated with Athens, Sparta, and Boeotia, where the Graces were honored as goddesses of beauty, charm, and the joys of festal life.

sections.heading: Depiction in art
paragraphs: In visual art Euphrosyne is most often shown alongside her sisters, the three Graces typically appearing as a dancing or intertwined trio. The motif recurs across the history of European art, notably in Sandro Botticelli's Primavera and in Antonio Canova's marble sculpture The Three Graces.
